claim: The eukaryotic genome is compacted into chromatin which is comprised of nucleosomes, each consisting of approximately 147 base pairs (bp) of DNA wound around a histone protein octamer.
source: The eukaryotic genome is compacted into chromatin (Kornberg, 1974) which is comprised of nucleosomes, each consisting of approximately 147 base pairs (bp) of DNA wound around a histone protein octamer (Kornberg and Lorch, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established scientific literature (Kornberg, 1974; Kornberg and Lorch, 1999), representing established scientific knowledge about chromatin structure.

claim: The helical DNA makes direct contact with the histones every 10 base pairs, with the major groove of DNA alternating between facing towards and away from the histone core.
source: The helical DNA makes direct contact with the histones every 10 base pairs, with the major groove of DNA alternating between facing towards and away from the histone core (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Luger et al., 1997, which describes the structural features of nucleosomes.

claim: Shifting the histones relative to the DNA sequence by a few base pairs can change the accessibility of sequence elements to DNA binding proteins.
source: Shifting the histones relative to the DNA sequence by a few base pairs can change the accessibility of sequence elements to DNA binding proteins if they are located in the linker sequences between nucleosomes, or may switch these elements between facing towards and away from nucleosomes if they are located within nucleosomal DNA (Jiang and Pugh, 2009b; Segal and Widom, 2009b; Zhang and Pugh, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Jiang and Pugh, 2009b; Segal and Widom, 2009b; Zhang and Pugh, 2011) describing the functional consequences of nucleosome positioning.

claim: Nucleosomes restrict the accessibility of DNA sequences to protein factors, such as transcriptional regulators and the transcription machinery.
source: Nucleosomes restrict the accessibility of DNA sequences to protein factors, such as transcriptional regulators and the transcription machinery (John et al., 2011; Li et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2006; Zhou and O'Shea, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing the role of nucleosomes in regulating DNA accessibility.

claim: The positions and occupancy of nucleosomes can influence the interplay between transcription factors and the level, dynamics, and differences in gene expression between cells.
source: The positions and occupancy of nucleosomes can influence the interplay between transcription factors (Mirny, 2010) and the level (Carey et al., 2013; Kim and O'Shea, 2008), dynamics (Lam et al., 2008), and differences in gene expression between cells (Dadiani et al., 2013; Raser and O'Shea, 2004; Tirosh and Barkai, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing various aspects of how nucleosome positioning affects gene expression.

claim: Nucleosome organization has been suggested to affect how gene promoters interpret dynamic signaling information at the single cell level.
source: Recently, nucleosome organization has also been suggested to affect how gene promoters interpret dynamic signaling information at the single cell level (Hansen and O'Shea, 2013; Hao and O'Shea, 2012), and heterogeneity in promoter nucleosome positions has been linked to differences in gene expression (Small et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies (Hansen and O'Shea, 2013; Hao and O'Shea, 2012; Small et al., 2014).

claim: Genome-wide nucleosome positions are commonly mapped with micrococcal nuclease digestion based high-throughput sequencing (MNase-seq).
source: Genome-wide nucleosome positions are commonly mapped with micrococcal nuclease digestion based high-throughput sequencing (MNase-seq) (Hughes and Rando, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation describing the common methodology for nucleosome mapping.

claim: MNase exhibits sequence preference when digesting DNA devoid of histones.
source: Although MNase exhibits sequence preference when digesting DNA devoid of histones (Horz and Altenburger, 1981), genome-wide analyses of nucleosomes with MNase-based methods are generally consistent with studies using MNase-independent methods (Hughes and Rando, 2014), such as DNase I chromatin digestion (Hesselberth et al., 2009) and chemical cleavage (Brogaard et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Horz and Altenburger, 1981, describing MNase sequence preference.

claim: Genome-wide analyses of nucleosomes with MNase-based methods are generally consistent with studies using MNase-independent methods.
source: Although MNase exhibits sequence preference when digesting DNA devoid of histones (Horz and Altenburger, 1981), genome-wide analyses of nucleosomes with MNase-based methods are generally consistent with studies using MNase-independent methods (Hughes and Rando, 2014), such as DNase I chromatin digestion (Hesselberth et al., 2009) and chemical cleavage (Brogaard et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations comparing MNase-based and MNase-independent methods.

claim: Studies that apply MNase-based methods typically report the position of a nucleosome as the average of the bulk nucleosome population (referred to as the 'consensus center').
source: Studies that apply MNase-based methods typically report the position of a nucleosome as the average of the bulk nucleosome population (referred to as the 'consensus center', Figure 1A) (Struhl and Segal, 2013; Zhang and Pugh, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations describing common practice in nucleosome mapping and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: If nucleosomes have overlapping positions in a significant portion of the population, the effect of averaging over heterogeneous nucleosome positions can lead to discrepancy between the consensus center of nucleosomes and the most representative nucleosome positions.
source: However, if nucleosomes have overlapping positions in a significant portion of the population, the effect of averaging over heterogeneous nucleosome positions can lead to discrepancy between the consensus center of nucleosomes and the most representative nucleosome positions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the consequences of averaging heterogeneous positions, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Determining the precise locations of individual nucleosomes within a cell population remains a challenge due to substantial variability in the mapped locations of digested nucleosomes.
source: A variety of methods have been developed to improve the precision of nucleosome mapping from MNase-seq data, such as peak finding of nucleosome occupancy (Zhang and Pugh, 2011) and filtering of single-end digestion patterns (Weiner et al., 2010), but determining the precise locations of individual nucleosomes within a cell population remains a challenge due to substantial variability in the mapped locations of digested nucleosomes – the midpoints of paired-end sequenced nucleosomes or the endpoints of single-end sequenced nucleosomes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to existing methods and is illustrated in Figure 1B showing the variability challenge.

claim: Variability in mapped nucleosome locations may arise from a cluster of overlapping and stably positioned nucleosomes, as well as from effects causing different degrees of digestion of the same nucleosome by MNase, such as nucleosome breathing and nuclease trimming.
source: This variability may arise from a cluster of overlapping and stably positioned nucleosomes, as well as from effects causing different degrees of digestion of the same nucleosome by MNase, such as nucleosome breathing and nuclease trimming – all of which influence the distribution of the aligned reads and are difficult to disentangle (Clark, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents inference about the sources of variability in MNase-seq data.

claim: A chemical cleavage approach that uses a genetically engineered histone H4 to chemically cleave DNA sequences in contact with the nucleosome dyad allowed direct measurement of nucleosome positions with unprecedented resolution.
source: Recently, a chemical cleavage approach that uses a genetically engineered histone H4 to chemically cleave DNA sequences in contact with the nucleosome dyad allowed direct measurement of nucleosome positions with unprecedented resolution (Brogaard et al., 2012; Moyle-Heyrman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing the chemical cleavage method.

claim: The requirement for genetic engineering of essential histones limits the current application of the chemical cleavage approach to genetically tractable organisms.
source: However, the requirement for genetic engineering of essential histones limits its current application to genetically tractable organisms.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the limitations of the chemical cleavage method.

claim: The authors developed a computational approach to determine in vivo nucleosome positions from paired-end MNase-sequencing data.
source: Here, we report a computational approach to determine in vivo nucleosome positions from paired-end MNase-sequencing data.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the manuscript describing the authors' methodological contribution.

claim: The authors use the size distribution of MNase digested nucleosome fragments to infer a digestion variability template for nucleosomes.
source: Inspired by this, we use the size distribution of MNase digested nucleosome fragments to infer a digestion variability template for nucleosomes, and report a Bayesian method that makes use of these templates to identify the individual positions of nucleosomes at a base-pair resolution, hereafter referred to as the template-based Bayesian (TBB) approach.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach developed in the study.

claim: The template-based Bayesian (TBB) approach can identify the individual positions of nucleosomes at a base-pair resolution.
source: Inspired by this, we use the size distribution of MNase digested nucleosome fragments to infer a digestion variability template for nucleosomes, and report a Bayesian method that makes use of these templates to identify the individual positions of nucleosomes at a base-pair resolution, hereafter referred to as the template-based Bayesian (TBB) approach.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the capability of the TBB method.

claim: The TBB approach can be applied to data generated through both paired-end and single-end sequencing to map chromatin structure in diverse organisms.
source: This approach can be applied to data generated through both paired-end and single-end sequencing to map chromatin structure in diverse organisms.
evidence: This claim describes the applicability of the method based on the authors' analysis.

claim: The periodic occurrences of dinucleotide sequence motifs relative to the nucleosome dyad can be directly determined from MNase based nucleosome positions and are conserved in vivo in both yeast and human cells.
source: We show that the periodic occurrences of dinucleotide sequence motifs relative to the nucleosome dyad can be directly determined from MNase based nucleosome positions and are conserved in vivo in both yeast and human cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on data analysis.

claim: Alternative configurations of nucleosomes are a common feature in both yeast and human chromatin.
source: Leveraging this method, we find that alternative configurations of nucleosomes are a common feature in both yeast and human chromatin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on data analysis using the TBB method.

claim: Alternatively positioned nucleosomes around gene transcription start sites represent configurations that differ in their compatibility with the assembly of the pre-initiation complex.
source: The alternatively positioned nucleosomes around gene transcription start sites represent configurations that differ in their compatibility with the assembly of the pre-initiation complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on data analysis and inference.

claim: A 3-step model for transcription initiation can reconcile the competition between nucleosomes and the transcriptional machinery observed from genomic analysis.
source: A 3-step model for transcription initiation can reconcile the competition between nucleosomes and the transcriptional machinery observed from genomic analysis.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their data analysis and inference.

claim: The authors generated paired-end data sets of 'T1' and 'T2', each with a coverage of ~2.8 read midpoints per base pair.
source: We generated paired-end data sets of 'T1' and 'T2', each with a coverage of ~2.8 read midpoints per base pair; as an average between these two data sets, we identified ~61,800 consensus centers of nucleosomes and ~125,000 TBB nucleosome positions, covering at least 75.5% of the S. cerevisiae genome.
evidence: This describes the experimental data generated in the study.

claim: As an average between the T1 and T2 data sets, the authors identified ~61,800 consensus centers of nucleosomes and ~125,000 TBB nucleosome positions, covering at least 75.5% of the S. cerevisiae genome.
source: We generated paired-end data sets of 'T1' and 'T2', each with a coverage of ~2.8 read midpoints per base pair; as an average between these two data sets, we identified ~61,800 consensus centers of nucleosomes and ~125,000 TBB nucleosome positions, covering at least 75.5% of the S. cerevisiae genome.
evidence: This describes the results of applying the TBB method to the experimental data.

claim: The spacing between adjacent TBB nucleosome positions peaked at 11 and 21 bp.
source: The spacing between adjacent TBB nucleosome positions peaked at 11 and 21 bp (Figure 1D), consistent with the rotation of DNA sequence by one or two helical turns around histone cores (Albert et al., 2007; Brogaard et al., 2012), and suggesting that the same nucleosome commonly occupies overlapping configurations in different cells.
evidence: This is a data-based finding shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The spacing between adjacent TBB nucleosome positions is consistent with the rotation of DNA sequence by one or two helical turns around histone cores.
source: The spacing between adjacent TBB nucleosome positions peaked at 11 and 21 bp (Figure 1D), consistent with the rotation of DNA sequence by one or two helical turns around histone cores (Albert et al., 2007; Brogaard et al., 2012), and suggesting that the same nucleosome commonly occupies overlapping configurations in different cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data (Figure 1D) and citations to previous studies.

claim: The same nucleosome commonly occupies overlapping configurations in different cells.
source: The spacing between adjacent TBB nucleosome positions peaked at 11 and 21 bp (Figure 1D), consistent with the rotation of DNA sequence by one or two helical turns around histone cores (Albert et al., 2007; Brogaard et al., 2012), and suggesting that the same nucleosome commonly occupies overlapping configurations in different cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed spacing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The consensus centers of nucleosomes identified by the template-based Bayesian approach were consistent with published methods employing Gaussian smoothing algorithms.
source: The consensus centers of nucleosomes identified by the template-based Bayesian approach were consistent with the published methods employing Gaussian smoothing algorithms (often referred to as 'Parzen window') (Albert et al., 2007, 2008; Clark, 2010; Tsankov et al., 2010) (Figure 2A), with more than 90% of the nucleosomes matching within a single base pair (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a validation of the method based on comparison with existing methods, supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: More than 90% of the nucleosomes identified by the TBB approach match within a single base pair with those identified by Parzen window methods.
source: The consensus centers of nucleosomes identified by the template-based Bayesian approach were consistent with the published methods employing Gaussian smoothing algorithms (often referred to as 'Parzen window') (Albert et al., 2007, 2008; Clark, 2010; Tsankov et al., 2010) (Figure 2A), with more than 90% of the nucleosomes matching within a single base pair (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding based on data comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The consensus centers identified by the TBB approach showed general agreement with published nucleosome reference maps.
source: These consensus centers also showed general agreement with the published nucleosome reference maps (Jiang and Pugh, 2009a) (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3), validating the overall biological relevance of our data sets.
evidence: This is a validation based on comparison with published reference maps, shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The nucleosome positions identified by the TBB approach and the chemical approach were consistent.
source: We then evaluated the accuracy of our identified TBB nucleosome positions by comparing them to individual nucleosome positions mapped through a recently reported chemical approach (Brogaard et al., 2012), which provides a reference that is independent of MNase cleavage specificity. The nucleosome positions identified by these two approaches were consistent (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4), demonstrating that the TBB approach can precisely map the positions of individual nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a validation based on comparison with an independent method, shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The TBB approach can precisely map the positions of individual nucleosomes.
source: The nucleosome positions identified by these two approaches were consistent (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4), demonstrating that the TBB approach can precisely map the positions of individual nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the validation data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The majority of the TBB nucleosome positions identified in simulated data sets were within 2–3 bp of the originally simulated nucleosome positions.
source: The majority of the TBB nucleosome positions identified in these simulated data sets were within 2–3 bp of the originally simulated nucleosome positions, even for the cases where nucleosome positions were separated by only 10–15 bp or differ by more than 3-fold in their relative occupancy (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico validation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Both the consensus centers and the TBB nucleosome positions were in agreement between the T1 and T2 experiments, with a median difference of 2 bp across the genome.
source: Both the consensus centers and the TBB nucleosome positions were in agreement between these two experiments (Figure 2D–E, Figure 2—figure supplements 5–6), with a median difference of 2 bp across the genome; in comparison, randomly generated consensus centers and nucleosome positions gave rise to a median difference of 49 bp and 36 bp, respectively.
evidence: This is a reproducibility finding based on comparison between two independent experiments, shown in Figure 2D-E and supplementary figures.

claim: Individual nucleosome positions can be reliably detected regardless of the differences in MNase digestion.
source: Individual nucleosome positions can be reliably detected regardless of the differences in MNase digestion (Figure 2F), demonstrating the robustness of the determined nucleosome positions to digestion variability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: When DNA sequences were aligned at the TBB nucleosome positions in yeast, the dinucleotide AA/AT/TA/TT and CC/CG/GC/GG motifs displayed 10 bp periodicity across almost the full length of the nucleosome core.
source: In contrast, when we aligned DNA sequences at the TBB nucleosome positions in yeast, the dinucleotide AA/AT/TA/TT and CC/CG/GC/GG motifs displayed 10 bp periodicity across almost the full length of the nucleosome core (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3), illustrating the power of the TBB approach to precisely map nucleosome positions from MNase-based methods.
evidence: This is a finding based on sequence analysis of TBB-identified positions, shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: After corrections for MNase digestion bias, dinucleotide AA/AT/TA/TT and CC/CG/GC/GG motifs displayed 10 bp periodicity.
source: After these corrections, we observed dinucleotide AA/AT/TA/TT and CC/CG/GC/GG motifs displaying 10 bp periodicity (Figure 4C), consistent with the dinucleotide frequency around the chemically determined nucleosome positions in yeast (Brogaard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding after correction for MNase bias, shown in Figure 4C and validated by comparison with chemical mapping data.

claim: Randomly shifting the determined TBB nucleosome positions by an average of 2 bp greatly reduced the observed dinucleotide periodicity and shifting the positions by an average of 5 bp completely eliminated the periodic pattern.
source: Randomly shifting the determined TBB nucleosome positions by an average of 2 bp greatly reduced the observed dinucleotide periodicity and shifting the positions by an average of 5 bp completely eliminated the periodic pattern (Figure 4D), demonstrating the importance of precisely mapping nucleosome positions in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding from a control experiment shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The frequency of AA/AT/TA/TT and CC/CG/GC/GG motifs displayed clear 10 bp periodicity relative to human TBB nucleosome positions, which was comparable to the motif periodicity observed in yeast.
source: The frequency of AA/AT/TA/TT and CC/CG/GC/GG motifs displayed clear 10 bp periodicity relative to human TBB nucleosome positions, which was comparable to the motif periodicity observed in yeast (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of human nucleosome data, shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: When DNA sequences were aligned at the consensus centers of human nucleosomes, the frequency of these dinucleotide motifs did not exhibit a clear periodicity with respect to the consensus centers.
source: In contrast, when DNA sequences were aligned at the consensus centers of human nucleosomes, the frequency of these dinucleotide motifs did not exhibit a clear periodicity with respect to the consensus centers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of consensus centers shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The TBB nucleosome positions exhibited a bimodal shape for at least three quarters of the genes with nucleosome-covered TSSs.
source: The TBB nucleosome positions exhibited a bimodal shape for at least three quarters of the genes with nucleosome-covered TSSs (Figure 5C, 'positions'), suggesting that alternative positioning is a common feature of nucleosomes near TSSs.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of nucleosome positions at TSSs, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Alternative positioning is a common feature of nucleosomes near TSSs.
source: The TBB nucleosome positions exhibited a bimodal shape for at least three quarters of the genes with nucleosome-covered TSSs (Figure 5C, 'positions'), suggesting that alternative positioning is a common feature of nucleosomes near TSSs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the bimodal distribution observed in Figure 5C.

claim: The occupancy of nucleosome midpoints at each gene correlated well between two experiments (T1 and T2).
source: The occupancy of nucleosome midpoints at each gene correlated well between two experiments (T1 and T2), indicating alternative nucleosomes can be reliably observed (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a reproducibility finding shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Most groups of overlapping nucleosomes showed less than 2-fold variation in the read occupancy between alternative TBB nucleosome positions.
source: When we examined the midpoints attributed to each nucleosome position within each group (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2), we found that most groups showed less than 2-fold variation in the read occupancy between alternative TBB nucleosome positions, suggesting that the different positions are significantly represented in the cell population and therefore are likely of biological relevance.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The different alternative nucleosome positions are significantly represented in the cell population and therefore are likely of biological relevance.
source: When we examined the midpoints attributed to each nucleosome position within each group (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2), we found that most groups showed less than 2-fold variation in the read occupancy between alternative TBB nucleosome positions, suggesting that the different positions are significantly represented in the cell population and therefore are likely of biological relevance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the occupancy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Alternative nucleosome positions were not a consequence of differential digestion at nucleosome edges.
source: These alternative positions were not a consequence of differential digestion at nucleosome edges (Weiner et al., 2010), as both ends of paired-end sequencing reads showed two peaks that match the edges of alternatively positioned nucleosomes (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on analysis of read ends shown in Figure 5E, with citation to Weiner et al., 2010 for context.

claim: Approximately one quarter of genes with their TSSs covered by nucleosomes contain more than two TBB nucleosome positions at TSSs.
source: Of the genes with their TSSs covered by nucleosomes, approximately one quarter contain more than two TBB nucleosome positions at TSSs, suggesting that chromatin structure at the transcription initiation site is complex and heterogeneous.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Chromatin structure at the transcription initiation site is complex and heterogeneous.
source: Of the genes with their TSSs covered by nucleosomes, approximately one quarter contain more than two TBB nucleosome positions at TSSs, suggesting that chromatin structure at the transcription initiation site is complex and heterogeneous.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that many genes have multiple nucleosome positions at TSSs.

claim: The unique, proximal and distal nucleosomes were digested by MNase to similar sizes.
source: The unique, proximal and distal nucleosomes were digested by MNase to similar sizes, further suggesting that the alternative nucleosome positions are not a result of MNase digestion bias (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Among uniquely positioned nucleosomes, TSSs were enriched ~10 bp inside the boundary of the nucleosome core.
source: Among uniquely positioned nucleosomes, TSSs weree enriched ~10 bp inside the boundary of the nucleosome core (Figure 6A, magenta curve).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Among the alternatively positioned nucleosomes, the proximal nucleosomes were located much closer to the TSS where the nucleosome core restricts the accessibility of these factors and therefore competes for active transcription.
source: Among the alternatively positioned nucleosomes, the proximal nucleosomes were located much closer to the TSS where the nucleosome core restricts the accessibility of these factors and therefore competes for active transcription (Figure 6A, cyan curve).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis shown in Figure 6A with inference about functional consequences.

claim: For the distal nucleosomes, TSSs were aligned near the edge of the nucleosome core, making these sites and the upstream regulatory elements accessible to other DNA binding factors.
source: For the distal nucleosomes, TSSs were aligned near the edge of the nucleosome core (Figure 6A, red curve), making these sites and the upstream regulatory elements accessible to other DNA binding factors.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis shown in Figure 6A with inference about accessibility.

claim: Most subunits of the PIC, including TBP, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF, TFIIH and TFIIK, showed peak enrichment at the edge of the distally positioned nucleosome.
source: Most subunits of the PIC, including TBP, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF, TFIIH and TFIIK, showed peak enrichment at the edge of the distally positioned nucleosome (Figure 6B, cyan), suggesting that the +1 nucleosome in the distal position marks a boundary for the assembly of the PIC.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of PIC occupancy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The +1 nucleosome in the distal position marks a boundary for the assembly of the PIC.
source: Most subunits of the PIC, including TBP, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF, TFIIH and TFIIK, showed peak enrichment at the edge of the distally positioned nucleosome (Figure 6B, cyan), suggesting that the +1 nucleosome in the distal position marks a boundary for the assembly of the PIC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PIC occupancy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The proximally positioned nucleosome covered most of the regions enriched for PIC binding.
source: In contrast, the proximally positioned nucleosome covered most of the regions enriched for PIC binding (Figure 6B, red), suggesting that the +1 nucleosome in the proximal position is not compatible with the binding of transcription machinery.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The +1 nucleosome in the proximal position is not compatible with the binding of transcription machinery.
source: In contrast, the proximally positioned nucleosome covered most of the regions enriched for PIC binding (Figure 6B, red), suggesting that the +1 nucleosome in the proximal position is not compatible with the binding of transcription machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap between proximal nucleosomes and PIC binding regions shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TATA-box and TATA-like sequences were enriched in front of the proximal nucleosomes.
source: Intriguingly, TATA-box and TATA-like sequences were enriched in front of the proximal nucleosomes (Figure 6C), suggesting that proximal nucleosomes do not block recognition of most TATA elements.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Proximal nucleosomes do not block recognition of most TATA elements.
source: Intriguingly, TATA-box and TATA-like sequences were enriched in front of the proximal nucleosomes (Figure 6C), suggesting that proximal nucleosomes do not block recognition of most TATA elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of TATA sequences relative to proximal nucleosomes shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The proximal nucleosome may represent a promoter state that is not associated with active transcription and is populated prior to the assembly of the PIC.
source: Thus, the proximal nucleosome may represent a promoter state that is not associated with active transcription and is populated prior to the assembly of the PIC (Figure 6D, Proximal state).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data, illustrated in Figure 6D.

claim: The distal nucleosome may represent a promoter state in the process of transcription initiation.
source: The distal nucleosome may represent a promoter state in the process of transcription initiation (Figure 6D, Distal state).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data, illustrated in Figure 6D.

claim: Genes with uniquely positioned nucleosomes at their TSSs were enriched in highly expressed genes.
source: We found that genes with uniquely positioned nucleosomes at their TSSs were enriched in highly expressed genes (Newman et al., 2006) (top 500 genes, p = 0.001, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis comparing nucleosome configurations with gene expression data.

claim: 73% of the genes encoding ribosomal proteins had TSSs with uniquely positioned nucleosomes.
source: More strikingly, we found that 73% of the genes encoding ribosomal proteins had TSSs with uniquely positioned nucleosomes (p<0.00001, Fisher's exact test), highlighting a connection between the configuration of nucleosomes (unique vs alternative) and gene expression.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: There is a connection between the configuration of nucleosomes (unique vs alternative) and gene expression.
source: More strikingly, we found that 73% of the genes encoding ribosomal proteins had TSSs with uniquely positioned nucleosomes (p<0.00001, Fisher's exact test), highlighting a connection between the configuration of nucleosomes (unique vs alternative) and gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of unique nucleosomes at highly expressed genes.

claim: The frequency of dinucleotides occurred periodically ~10 bp from the positions of either proximal or distal nucleosomes and resembled the periodic feature of nucleosomes in yeast genome.
source: The frequency of dinucleotides occurred periodically ~10 bp from the positions of either proximal or distal nucleosomes and resembled the periodic feature of nucleosomes in yeast genome (R2 = 0.75, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Dinucleotide periodicity was less pronounced in the uniquely positioned nucleosomes.
source: This periodicity was less pronounced in the uniquely positioned nucleosomes (R2 = 0.40 between dinucleotide frequency in uniquely positioned nucleosomes and all nucleosomes in yeast genome; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Autocorrelation analysis of the dinucleotide frequency revealed a lack of periodicity in DNA sequences around the uniquely positioned nucleosomes.
source: Autocorrelation analysis of the dinucleotide frequency revealed a lack of periodicity in DNA sequences around the uniquely positioned nucleosomes, further highlighting the difference between uniquely and alternatively positioned nucleosomes (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The uniquely positioned nucleosomes were flanked by a strong enrichment of poly(dA:dT)6 sequences.
source: When we examined the occurrences of poly(dA:dT) sequences at least 6 nucleotides in length, we found that the uniquely positioned nucleosomes were flanked by a strong enrichment of poly(dA:dT)6 sequences (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A similar but weaker enrichment of poly(dA:dT)6 sequences was observed flanking both the proximally and the distally positioned nucleosomes.
source: A similar but weaker enrichment of poly(dA:dT)6 sequences was also observed flanking both the proximally and the distally positioned nucleosomes (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Uniquely positioned nucleosomes and alternatively positioned nucleosomes presented different DNA sequence features.
source: Overall, uniquely positioned nucleosomes and alternatively positioned nucleosomes presented different DNA sequence features, suggesting that these sequence determinants may contribute to the different configurations of chromatin states at gene promoters.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the sequence analysis data.

claim: DNA sequence determinants may contribute to the different configurations of chromatin states at gene promoters.
source: Overall, uniquely positioned nucleosomes and alternatively positioned nucleosomes presented different DNA sequence features, suggesting that these sequence determinants may contribute to the different configurations of chromatin states at gene promoters.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed sequence differences.
